newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech cap market watchdog bill seen in mid-1997.
newsitem.headline: Czech cap market watchdog bill seen in mid-1997.

text.p: The Czech parliament's budget committee may submit its own bill on re-regulating securities markets as early as February if an acceptable plan does not come from the government, a committee member said on Wednesday.

The budget committee plan, which would include creating a U.S.-style Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), would be a "deputies' proposal" if a compromise plan is not put forward soon by the Finance Ministry, Tomas Pav, a deputy of the ruling coalition on the budget committee, told Reuters.
"We would like to do this as quickly as possible, but there are certain timetables we can't omit," Pav said.

"We want to have it in a proper legislative form, including expert defences (of the plan), in parliament during February. It most probably would be a deputies' proposal," said Pav who is a member of the ruling Civic Democratic Party (ODS).

Pav said that Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik, who has been cool to plans for market re-regulation, had been working on a ministry proposal and he did not exclude that a compromise could be submitted as a government plan.

A public row over capital market supervision and regulation has hotted up in recent days, pitting Prague Stock Exchange Chairman Tomas Jezek, also a member of ODS, against the Finance Ministry, led by ODS colleague Kocarnik.

Jezek has led a move to set up an independent Czech SEC, funded by a transaction fee, and to concentrate trading on organised markets to reduce the pervasive off-market trades which are simply registered on the Central Securities Registry.
Investors have long complained that Czech share prices are unreliable because of the off-market concentration of trades, and that insider trading is rampant.

A bill executing the plans backed by Jezek, who is a former chairman of the budget committee, appears to have the solid bi-partisan backing of the current committee leadership, including the chairman, Social Democrat Jozef Wagner.
But the Finance Ministry has balked at Jezek's ideas, especially Deputy Finance Minister Vladimir Rudlovcak who has opposed stricter regulation of Czech securities trading.

Rudlovcak on Wednesday defended the Czech system, telling the daily Mlada Fronta Dnes that the rules permitted unfettered trading of shares as in countries which allowed bearer shares to be traded "even in a cafe."
Pav said he did not share Jezek's optimism that a final bill would be enacted by the middle of 1997.
"At best, July of 1997," it could be approved, he said, but added that a September final approval was more realistic.
